title: Migrating a 7-Year Legacy ERP to a Medallion Data Warehouse using CDC and Zero Data Loss
summary: How we extracted MySQL binlogs with Change Data Capture, leveraged RabbitMQ idempotent workers, and reduced analytical query times by >70% with zero downtime.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.business-data-requirements: Operating for over 7 years, our legacy ERP database accumulated millions of retail and fulfillment transactions. The Business Intelligence (BI) team and executives required near-realtime dashboards to optimize inventory and marketing budgets. However, the operational MySQL database relied heavily on an Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) schema. Running heavy multi-table joins on OLTP exhausted CPU resources and threatened order processing throughput.
sections.data-modeling:
Rather than querying transactional tables directly, we adopted a multi-tier Medallion Architecture separating OLAP from OLTP:

  • Bronze Layer (Raw Ingestion): Append-only tables preserving unmodified JSON payload events captured from MySQL binlogs.
  • Silver Layer (Cleaned & Conformed): Validated 3NF schemas with normalized types, deduplicated events, and cleansed foreign key references.
  • Gold Layer (Dimensional Star Schema): High-performance Fact and Dimension tables optimized for analytical reporting in Looker Studio.
sections.pipeline-construction:
The CDC ingestion pipeline was built without touching legacy ERP monolith code:

  • Binary Log Ingestion: Debezium/Canal captures MySQL row-based binlogs and streams change events into RabbitMQ topic exchanges.
  • Idempotent Go Workers: High-throughput Go consumers decode payloads and execute atomic PostgreSQL INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (UPSERT) operations.
  • Dead Letter Queue (DLX): Corrupted events or transient network issues route to a DLX with automated exponential backoff retries.
sections.testing-optimization:
Key validation and tuning strategies included:

  • Automated Reconciliation: Nightly checksum audits at 02:00 AM comparing record counts and aggregate hashes between MySQL and PostgreSQL.
  • Performance Tuning: Monthly table partitioning, BRIN indexes on timestamp columns, and micro-batching worker writes (500 records/batch).
  • Pipeline Latency: End-to-end sync latency from OLTP commit to DW availability remained under 1.8 seconds under peak load.
sections.summary-recommendations: The solution achieved a 96% data reconciliation rate with 0% data loss, decreased analytical query times by over 70%, and eliminated ERP database locking. Recommendation: Always enforce idempotent consumer writes and schema versioning when designing event-driven CDC architectures.

title: Architecting High-Throughput Event Ingestion with Spring WebFlux, Kafka & Automated PII Masking
summary: Building a privacy-compliant MarTech analytics gateway that handles thousands of real-time e-commerce conversion events with sub-second latency.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.context-problem: During flash sales and peak marketing campaigns, e-commerce traffic surges by 15x–20x. The tracking gateway must reliably capture tens of thousands of customer micro-events per second (cart additions, voucher clicks, product views) and relay them to Google Analytics 4 and Facebook Conversions API. Traditional synchronous architectures caused thread exhaustion and sluggish checkout experiences.
sections.system-requirements:
• Functional: Ingest, validate, cleanse, and route tracking events in real time to external marketing partners.
  • Non-Functional: p99 API response time < 15ms, sustain 10,000 RPS throughput, strict PII privacy compliance (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP), and zero message loss during partner outages.
sections.architecture-design:
We designed an asynchronous, non-blocking Reactive Event-Driven architecture:

  • Ingestion Layer: Spring WebFlux (Project Reactor over Netty) ingests requests asynchronously and immediately buffers payloads to an Apache Kafka cluster.
  • Privacy & Sanitization: Custom Spring AOP interceptors and Jackson serializers recursively mask sensitive PII (emails, phone numbers, identity numbers) using salted SHA-256 hashing.
  • Outbound Delivery: Consumer microservices read from Kafka and dispatch payload batches via non-blocking Spring WebClient.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Evaluating Synchronous MVC vs. Reactive WebFlux:

  • Traditional Spring MVC (Thread-per-request): Straightforward debugging, but high concurrency leads to thread starvation and memory bloat under 5,000+ concurrent connections.
  • Reactive Non-Blocking (Spring WebFlux): Steeper learning curve for reactive stream debugging, but scales effortlessly across 20,000+ RPS using minimal CPU threads and 60% less heap memory.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Integrate Resilience4j Circuit Breakers and rate limiters on outbound ad connectors to isolate upstream latency. Never invoke blocking JDBC or file I/O operations directly within the reactive Event Loop.

title: Scaling an ERP Customer Reporting Portal to 1,000+ Concurrent Users with Redis & Node.js
summary: Techniques for caching heavy reporting queries, batch synchronization, and designing modular UI component architectures.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.context-problem: An enterprise reporting portal served over 1,000 corporate clients logging in concurrently between 08:00 and 09:30 AM. Each client requested multi-dimensional performance reports. Under morning peak load, database CPU utilization reached 100%, page response times degraded beyond 10 seconds, and users experienced frequent HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts.
sections.system-requirements:
• Functional: Render customizable reporting views, dynamic date filters, channel breakdowns, and interactive data visualizations.
  • Non-Functional: Sub-second page load times (< 800ms), support 1,000+ active concurrent clients, maximum data staleness under 5 minutes, and efficient cloud resource utilization.
sections.architecture-design:
We engineered a decoupled caching and asynchronous rendering architecture:

  • Cache-Aside with Redis: Heavy analytical aggregations are cached in a Redis Cluster with structured key namespacing and dynamic TTLs aligned with data refresh frequencies.
  • Modular UI Components: Independent Vue.js charting widgets render asynchronously using skeleton loaders, preventing blocking UI render cascades.
  • Query Batching & Deduplication: Node.js backend batches identical queries within a 50ms window (DataLoader pattern), collapsing redundant database requests into a single query execution.
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Comparing Database Read Replicas vs. Distributed Redis Caching:

  • Read Replicas: High infrastructure overhead and still vulnerable to expensive full-table aggregation spikes without proper caching.
  • Redis Caching + Query Batching: Cut infrastructure costs by 80%, eliminated 90% of direct database load, with an acceptable 2-minute cache invalidation window for analytical metrics.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Implement Cache Stampede Prevention via distributed mutexes or probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) to prevent simultaneous database hammering on cache misses. Always enforce strict connection pool timeouts.

title: Optimizing Multi-Stage Docker (<25MB) & Building Zero-Downtime CI/CD with GitHub Actions
summary: Ultralight container packaging on Alpine, Nginx SPA fallback routing, and automated static typechecks in delivery pipelines.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.article-objectives: Provide a comprehensive guide to building ultralight SPA container images (< 25MB) using Docker Multi-Stage builds on Alpine Linux, combined with an automated GitHub Actions CI/CD workflow to achieve seamless, zero-downtime production delivery.
sections.architecture-principles:
The containerization architecture decouples compilation from production serving:

  • Stage 1 (Build Environment): Uses node:20-alpine to install packages, run TypeScript typechecks, and compile static production bundles into /dist.
  • Stage 2 (Runtime Server): Copies only the compiled /dist artifacts into nginx:alpine-slim (< 15MB) with custom caching headers, gzip compression, and SPA fallback routing.
  • GitHub Actions CI/CD: Triggered on commits and PRs, automating Lint -> Test -> Build -> Docker Registry Push -> Zero-Downtime Server Reload.
sections.step-by-step-setup:
Implementation steps:

  • Step 1: Create a multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root execution and comprehensive .dockerignore rules.
  • Step 2: Configure nginx.conf with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; and immutable caching policies for hashed assets.
  • Step 3: Author .github/workflows/deploy.yml leveraging GitHub Actions Cache and Docker Buildx to accelerate build times by 3x.
sections.troubleshooting-pitfalls:
• 404 errors on browser refresh: Missing SPA fallback routing in Nginx. Resolved by adding try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html.
  • Bloated Docker images: Caused by accidental bundling of node_modules or omitting the runtime copy stage.
  • Security vulnerabilities: Running containers as root. Always configure non-root users (USER nginx).
sections.evaluation-scaling: Reduced container image size from 850MB to 22MB and deployment latency from 6 minutes down to 45 seconds. Future roadmap: Incorporate Trivy vulnerability scanning into PR checks and establish Kubernetes Canary rollouts.

title: Idempotency & Concurrency Control in Distributed Workers with Go & Redis
summary: Reliable message processing with Distributed Locks, Dedup Keys, and graceful failure handling without goroutine leaks.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.problem-statement: In distributed worker architectures, messaging systems (RabbitMQ, Kafka) operate on At-Least-Once delivery semantics. During transient network hiccups or consumer pod restarts, payment and order update messages can be delivered multiple times, risking race conditions and duplicate financial deductions.
sections.initial-approach: A simple "Check-then-Act" pattern checks database state prior to execution. In multi-worker environments, however, concurrent goroutines frequently read the "PENDING" status simultaneously, both proceeding to process the duplicate event and corrupting state.
sections.optimization-thinking:
We engineered a resilient, two-tiered idempotency model:

  • Distributed Locks via Redis: Atomic SET lock_key worker_id NX PX 5000 operations ensure only a single worker executes the transaction block for a specific deduplication key.
  • Atomic State Transitions: Database updates enforce conditional state guards: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'PENDING'.
  • Graceful Shutdown: Goroutine lifecycles are bound to sync.WaitGroup and cancelable contexts, preventing abrupt termination of in-flight business transactions.
sections.code-implementation:
Go implementation of the idempotent distributed worker:

func (w *PaymentWorker) Process(ctx context.Context, msg Message) error {
    lockKey := fmt.Sprintf("lock:payment:%s", msg.PaymentID)
    acquired, err := w.redis.SetNX(ctx, lockKey, w.workerID, 10*time.Second).Result()
    if err != nil || !acquired {
        return nil // Skip processing if another worker holds the lock
    }
    defer w.redis.Del(ctx, lockKey)

    return w.db.Transaction(func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
        res, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, "UPDATE payments SET status = 'COMPLETED' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'PENDING'", msg.PaymentID)
        if err != nil { return err }
        rows, _ := res.RowsAffected()
        if rows == 0 { return nil } // Already processed idempotently
        return w.dispatchReceipt(ctx, msg)
    })
}
sections.complexity-applications: Time Complexity: O(1) Redis lock acquisition and O(1) indexed SQL execution. Widely applicable to e-commerce payment gateways, financial ledger syncs, ticketing platforms, and mission-critical event-driven architectures.

title: From Software Engineer to System Architect: Mindset, Trade-offs & Practical Lessons
summary: Field-tested reflections on balancing technical excellence with business value, making responsible architectural decisions, and sustained engineering growth.
author: Tan Huynh Nhat

sections.introduction: Transitioning from a Senior Software Engineer to a System Architect is not just a matter of accumulating years of experience. It represents a fundamental mindset shift: evolving from asking "How do I implement this code?" to "Why should we choose this approach, and what are its systemic consequences three years down the line?".
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Key differences between the two roles:

  • Problem Solving: Senior engineers strive for algorithm efficiency; architects navigate multi-dimensional trade-offs between cost, time-to-market, maintainability, and team capabilities.
  • Scope of Impact: Expands from individual microservices to the entire technical ecosystem and cross-functional alignment (Product, DevOps, Security).
  • Primary Toolkit: Evolves from IDEs and debuggers to Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), C4 Model diagrams, and clear technical articulation.
sections.case-study-experience: A real-world lesson from a premature microservice migration: Our team initially split a system into 20 microservices to "follow modern trends". The result was quadrupled operational overhead, distributed tracing complexity, and team fatigue. Re-evaluating the business reality, we consolidated into a clean Modular Monolith with targeted Event-Driven workers, cutting cloud expenses by 50% while doubling feature velocity.
sections.actionable-recommendations:
Three daily habits to cultivate architectural thinking:

  • Document ADRs for Major Decisions: Record the context, evaluated alternatives, decision rationale, and accepted compromises.
  • Study Industry Engineering Blogs: Read real-world architectural case studies from Netflix, Stripe, and Uber to understand high-scale patterns.
  • Practice System Design Reviews: Regularly sketch distributed architectures, challenge single points of failure, and analyze bottleneck resiliency.
sections.open-questions-discussion: In the era of rapid AI and cloud-native acceleration, should architects focus primarily on mastering low-level core engineering, or cultivate technical leadership and product strategy? Share your perspectives and real-world experiences!
